home.eyebrow: A free, open-source school of mathematics
home.title: Mathematics, from counting to categories — for everyone, everywhere.
home.lead: The Lumenary is a growing curriculum where every idea is explored three ways: understood by people, proved precisely, and tested by computation. Learn at your own pace. No accounts, no ads, no streaks.
home.modesTitle: Three ways of knowing, woven together
home.modesLead: Each concept is taught through three complementary modes that reinforce one another rather than living in separate books.
home.modeHText: Intuition, examples, pictures, conjectures and clear human proofs. Not just how — but why it’s true.
home.modeFText: Precise definitions and machine-checked proofs in Lean 4. Assumptions made explicit; nothing claimed that didn’t compile.
home.modeCText: Python experiments you can run in your browser. Learn the difference between evidence, approximation and proof.
home.sequenceLead: Five connected lessons, from sorting a basket of fruit to composing functions — the doorway to category theory.
home.trailsLead: Optional side-paths for the curious. They never count against you, and they always lead back to where you were.
home.entryLead: Every learner begins somewhere. Pick the door that fits — you can always wander.
home.principleQuote: Master the present. Glimpse the future. Never require the future to understand the present.
home.honestLead: The Lumenary is at the very beginning. Here is exactly what has been built and checked so far.
home.notYetReviewed: No content has yet been reviewed by a human mathematician or educator. That review is the next essential step.
home.valuesLead: Truthfulness, humility, generosity and wonder shape how The Lumenary is built — and every learner is welcome, whatever they believe.

lab.title: Math laboratory
lab.lead: Experiment, calculate, simulate — and learn what a computation can and cannot tell you. Every experiment runs in your browser and is also tested automatically.
lab.scratchLead: A blank Python sandbox with SymPy and NumPy available.
lab.ladderLead: Computers are wonderful at producing evidence. Proof is a different thing. Here is how the kinds of computational evidence differ.

ladder.exact: Arithmetic on integers or fractions with no rounding. The answer is exactly right — for the inputs computed.
ladder.symbolic: Algebra on symbols, like expanding (x + 1)². As trustworthy as the rules the software was built on.
ladder.exhaustive-finite: Checking every case of a finite problem. A genuine proof — but only for that finite set of cases.
ladder.counterexample: One case where a general claim fails. A single counterexample really does disprove a “for all” statement.
ladder.numerical: Floating-point approximations. Fast and useful, but rounding errors can creep in and must be understood.
ladder.experimental: Trying many examples. Builds confidence and suggests conjectures, but cannot prove a statement about infinitely many cases.
ladder.statistical: Estimates from random samples, with uncertainty. Tells us what is likely, never what is certain.
ladder.proof: A logical argument that covers every case. Human proofs explain why; Lean proofs are checked by a machine.

lab.experimentsLead: Every experiment in the curriculum, grouped by level. Open one to read, run and change its code.

formal.title: Formal mathematics laboratory
formal.lead: Lean 4 is a programming language and proof assistant: a computer checks every step of a proof. Here you can read every formal proof used by The Lumenary — and the exact report of what compiled.
formal.whatIsText: A declaration is labelled formally verified only if it appears in the latest Lean build report, compiled without errors, and does not depend on sorry. We also list which axioms each proof relies on.
formal.scope: Elementary modules (Kindergarten to Grade 8) use core Lean 4 only; later modules build on Mathlib, at the version shown in the build report. Each declaration records whether it applies an existing library theorem or is proved here.
formal.exercisesLead: Each exercise contains a sorry for you to replace. Open it in the Lean web editor, or clone the repository and run lake build.
formal.modulesLead: Each lesson has its own Lean module. Open one to read every declaration with its axioms and provenance, and to try its exercises.

sort.title: The market sorting game
sort.subtitle: Pick something from the basket, then pick the box it belongs in.
sort.empty: The basket is empty — everything has been sorted!
sort.nowPick: Now choose a box for the {item}.
sort.lookAgain: Look again at the {item}. Which box does it belong in?
sort.successColour: Wonderful! You made five collections — and one of them is empty. An empty box is still a collection.
sort.successShape: Wonderful! Every item is in exactly one collection.

venn.title: Shade a set, discover its name
venn.subtitle: Click regions of the diagram (or use the buttons). The explorer names the set you have made and lists its elements.
venn.diagram: Venn diagram of A and B inside the universe U
venn.challenge: Challenge: two regions can be shaded in six different ways. Can you find all six, and name each one?

int.title: Walking the number line
int.subtitle: Adding a negative number walks to the left. Every integer has an opposite that walks you home to zero.
int.home: You came home to 0! The number you added is the opposite of where you started.
int.addHint: Can you find the number that brings you exactly home to 0?
int.twice: The opposite of the opposite is where you started: −(−a) = a.
int.flipHint: Taking the opposite reflects through zero. What happens if you do it twice?

arrow.title: Draw a function
arrow.subtitle: Click an element of A, then an element of B, to draw an arrow. Click the same pair again to remove it.
arrow.diagram: Arrow diagram from A to B
arrow.howTo: Click an element of A to start an arrow.
arrow.isFunction: Is it a function from A to B?
arrow.isFunctionYes: Yes: every element of A has exactly one arrow.
arrow.tooMany: {x} has more than one arrow — a function gives exactly one output.
arrow.noArrow: {x} has no arrow yet — a function needs an output for every input.
arrow.injectiveYes: No two arrows land on the same element.
arrow.surjectiveYes: Every element of B is hit.
arrow.bijectiveYes: A perfect pairing: you could reverse every arrow.
arrow.pigeonhole: With {m} inputs and only {n} outputs, two arrows must land together — so no function A → B can be injective. This is the pigeonhole principle.

comp.title: Composition machines
comp.subtitle: Feed a number through two machines. Does the order matter?
comp.sameEverywhere: Both orders agree for every input from −5 to 5. (Checking a range is evidence — can you prove they always agree?)
comp.sameHere: They agree for this input — but try others. Agreement at one input doesn’t mean the functions are equal.
comp.different: Different results: {a} versus {b}. The order of composition matters.
comp.goldIs: Gold dashed arrows show g ∘ f, which goes straight from A to C.
comp.chainNote: Change f or g and watch g ∘ f update. To compute (g ∘ f)(x), follow the arrow from x to B, then from there to C.

inv.title: The partner search
inv.subtitle: For each integer a, search for a partner b that brings you back to the identity.
inv.zero: Zero times anything is 0, never 1. Zero has no multiplicative partner in any number system.
inv.none: No integer works — and searching further wouldn’t help (can you see why?).
inv.fraction: Outside the integers there is a partner: b = {b}. Fractions fix the problem the integers can’t.
inv.onlyOnes: Among the integers, only 1 and −1 have multiplicative partners.

clock.title: The clock laboratory
clock.subtitle: On a clock with k hours, counting wraps around. Explore adding and multiplying.
clock.addNote: {sum} hours forward on a {k}-hour clock lands on {end}: the remainder when {sum} is divided by {k}.
clock.partners: Numbers with a multiplicative partner (a 1 in their row):
clock.pattern: These are exactly the numbers that share no common factor with k other than 1:

rem.title: Remainder families
rem.subtitle: Colour each integer by its remainder after dividing by k. Every integer lands in exactly one family.
rem.line: Integers from −15 to 15 coloured by remainder
rem.addTitle: Add a member of one family to a member of another…
rem.always: Every time, the sum lands in family [{r}]. The family of a sum depends only on the families — not on which members you picked.

boxes.title: Boxes inside boxes
boxes.subtitle: Start with one empty box. Build new collections by putting boxes into boxes.
boxes.wrap: Put it in a new box
boxes.together: Put them together in a box
boxes.howTo: Select one box to wrap, or several to put together.
boxes.already: You already have {set} — a collection is determined by what is inside, so this is the same box.
boxes.vonNeumann: Look at the boxes the magic wand builds: ∅ has 0 elements, {∅} has 1, {∅, {∅}} has 2… Each new box contains all the earlier ones. Some mathematicians use exactly these sets to define the counting numbers.

cat.title: Arrows that compose
cat.subtitle: Click arrows to build a path. Every path composes to a single arrow — and brackets never matter.
cat.cannot: Can’t compose: {last} ends at {end}, but {next} starts at {start}.
cat.brackets: Two ways to bracket h ∘ g ∘ f
cat.same: The last two columns always agree: h ∘ (g ∘ f) = (h ∘ g) ∘ f. That is associativity.

prod.title: The product, by its maps
prod.subtitle: Choose maps f : Z → A and g : Z → B. Then try to build a map h : Z → A × B that projects back to f and g.
prod.badFirst: First coordinates don’t match: h({z}) starts with {a}, but f({z}) = {fa}.
prod.badSecond: Second coordinates don’t match: h({z}) ends with {b}, but g({z}) = {gb}.
prod.challenge: Your turn: choose h(p), h(q), h(r) by clicking cells.
prod.unique: It works — and look: your h is exactly ⟨f, g⟩. There was only one possible choice. That uniqueness is what “universal” means.

diag.title: The diagonal machine
diag.subtitle: Here is a list of infinite 0–1 sequences (we can only show the start). The gold sequence d flips the diagonal.
diag.differs: d differs from s{i} in position {i}: s{i} has {a} there, d has {b}.
diag.hover: Point at (or tab to) a row to see where d differs from it. Click any digit to change the list.
diag.note: Add d to the list and a new d appears that is different again. No list — however long — can contain every sequence.

shapes.title: Shape explorer
shapes.subtitle: Pick a shape and switch on its features: sides, corners, angles, symmetry and diagonals.

note.equilateral: All three sides are equal and all three angles are 60°.
note.isosceles: Two sides are equal, and the two angles opposite them are equal too.
note.scalene: No two sides are equal and no two angles are equal. This one is also acute: every angle is less than 90°.
note.right: One angle is a right angle (90°). The longest side, opposite the right angle, is called the hypotenuse.
note.rightIsosceles: A right angle and two equal sides: the other two angles are both 45°.
note.obtuse: One angle is greater than 90°. A triangle can have at most one such angle.
note.square: Four equal sides and four right angles. A square is a special rectangle and also a special rhombus.
note.rectangle: Four right angles; opposite sides are equal and parallel. Its diagonals are equal in length.
note.rhombus: Four equal sides; opposite angles are equal. Its diagonals cross at right angles.
note.parallelogram: Two pairs of parallel sides; opposite sides and opposite angles are equal. It has no line of symmetry, but it looks the same after a half turn.
note.trapezoid: One pair of parallel sides. British English calls this a trapezium, American English a trapezoid. Books also differ on the definition: “exactly one pair of parallel sides” (then a parallelogram is not one) or “at least one pair” (then every parallelogram is one). Say which definition you use.
note.isoTrapezoid: A trapezium (trapezoid) whose two non-parallel sides are equal. It has one line of symmetry, and its base angles are equal.
note.kite: Two pairs of equal sides next to each other. One diagonal is a line of symmetry, and the diagonals cross at right angles.
note.regular: All sides are equal and all angles are equal. A regular polygon with n sides has n lines of symmetry and rotational symmetry of order n.
note.circle: Every point on a circle is the same distance, the radius, from the centre.

circle.sides: One curved edge, no straight sides
circle.fits: A circle fits onto its outline after any turn at all.

shapes.fitsAfter: It fits onto its dashed outline after every {deg}° turn: {k} times in one full turn.
shapes.fitsOnlyFull: It only fits onto its dashed outline after a full 360° turn.
shapes.hint: Switch on a feature above to see its facts.

legend.sides: Sides with the same number of ticks are equal.
legend.symmetry: Each dashed line is a line of symmetry: fold along it and the two halves match exactly.

poly.aria: cut from vertex A into {t} triangles
poly.triangle: A triangle is already a single triangle: its angles add up to 180°.
poly.cut: From vertex A, {d} diagonals cut the {name} into {t} triangles.
poly.sum: The angles of each triangle add up to 180°, and together they make up exactly the angles of the polygon. So the angle sum is
poly.anyConvex: This works for every convex polygon, regular or not: try Irregular.

area.title: Area and perimeter
area.subtitle: Area counts the unit squares inside a shape; perimeter measures the distance around it.
area.rows: {h} rows of {w} squares: multiply to count them all.
area.rectNote: Area is counted in unit squares. Perimeter is counted in unit lengths, all the way around the edge.

rect.aria: A {w} by {h} rectangle: area {a} square units, perimeter {p} units.

draw.hint: Click or tap squares to fill or empty them (with a mouse you can also drag). Arrow keys move between squares.
draw.empty: Start by filling in a few squares.
draw.pieces: Your shape is in {k} separate pieces.
draw.sameArea: Same area, different perimeters: knowing the area does not tell you the perimeter.

split.note: Two rectangles with the same height, side by side, make one big rectangle. So a × (b + c) = a × b + a × c: the distributive law.

tri.aria: A triangle with base {b} and height {h} inside a {b} by {h} rectangle: rectangle area {r}, triangle area {a} square units.
tri.note1: Each outside piece turns to fit exactly onto an inside piece. So the triangle is exactly half of its rectangle: ½ × base × height.
tri.note2: Slide the top corner along: the area does not change, because the base and the height stay the same.

clock2.title: Telling the time
clock2.subtitle: Move the long minute hand and watch the short hour hand follow.
clock2.amNote: a.m. means between midnight and noon.
clock2.pmNote: p.m. means between noon and midnight.
clock2.hidden: Digital time is hidden: read the clock first, then show it to check.
clock2.dragHint: Drag either hand, or use the buttons. When a hand has focus, the arrow keys move it.

elapsed.countOn: Count on: first to the next o'clock, then whole hours, then the minutes left over.
elapsed.turns: Full turns of the minute hand: {k} (each full turn is 60 minutes).

ruler.title: Measuring length
ruler.subtitle: Line an object up with the ruler. Where does it start, and where does it end?
ruler.subtitleClips: Measure with paper clips and hand spans. Why do we need standard units?
ruler.aria: Ruler from 0 to 20 centimetres, with an object to measure: {object}
ruler.dragHint: Drag the object, or use the buttons. When it has focus, the arrow keys move it.
ruler.question: How long is it?

fb.correct: Yes! It starts at {s} and ends at {e}, so it is {e} − {s} = {l} cm long.
fb.correctZero: Yes! It starts at 0 and ends at {e}, so it is {l} cm long.
fb.endReading: That is where it ends, but it does not start at 0. It starts at {s}, so its length is {e} − {s} = {l} cm. Or slide it to start at 0 and read the end.
fb.marks: Close! Count the spaces between the numbers (each space is 1 cm), not the marks.
fb.wrong: Not quite. Find where it starts and where it ends, then take the difference.

ruler.edgeNote: Careful: the end of a ruler is often not at 0. Line the object up with the 0 mark, or subtract the start.
ruler.why: The same object measures a different number of units when the unit changes, and hand spans differ from person to person. A centimetre is the same size everywhere, so a length in centimetres means the same to everybody.

pattern.title: Pattern maker
pattern.subtitle: Find the part that repeats, or the rule that makes a pattern grow.
pattern.core: The core: the part that repeats
pattern.addHint: Tap a shape to add it to the core:
pattern.coreFull: The core can have at most {max} items.

fb.wrong: Not quite. Try again, or press “Show how”.

pattern.how: The core has {len} items, so the pattern starts again after every {len} items.
pattern.howPos: The remainder gives the place in the core: item {k} is item {pos} of the core:
pattern.howZero: The remainder is 0, so item {k} is the last item of a core:
pattern.rule: Number of tiles in step n:

fbGrow.wrong: Not quite. Look at how the number of tiles changes from one step to the next.

pattern.firstDiff: The number of tiles changes by the same amount, {d}, at every step.
pattern.secondDiff: The change itself grows by the same amount, {d}, at every step: the sign of an n² term.

error.negative: This rule gives fewer than 0 tiles at step {n}. Choose a, b and c so that every step has 0 or more tiles.
error.tooMany: Only the first {k} steps are drawn: later steps have too many tiles to show.

data.title: Data explorer
data.subtitle: Show the same data as tallies, pictures, bars or dots, and find the mean, median and mode.
data.sampleNote: Example data: our class's favourite fruit.
data.empty: No data yet. Open “Change the data” to add some.
data.partialNote: Part of a picture stands for part of {k}: half a picture is half of {k}.
data.binNote: Each bar counts the values from its left edge up to, but not including, its right edge.
data.fairHint: Each tower shows one amount. Level them to share everything out fairly.
data.fairDone: Blocks moved from the tall towers (dashed) to the short ones (striped) until every tower is the same height. That fair share is the mean: {total} ÷ {count} {mean}.
data.meanCat: Mean (the fair share): total ÷ number of amounts
data.medianCat: Median: the middle amount when the amounts are sorted
data.medianNum: Median: the middle value when the values are sorted
data.medianOdd: It is value number {p} of {k} in the sorted list.
data.medianEven: There are two middle values, number {p} and number {q} of {k}; the median is halfway between them.
data.modeCatNone: No mode yet: every category is empty.
data.modeNum: Mode (the value that appears most often):
data.modeNone: No mode: every value appears just once.

spinner.title: Spinner
spinner.subtitle: Spin, keep a tally and compare the results with the sizes of the parts.
spinner.note: More spins usually bring the fraction of spins closer to the fraction of the spinner — usually, not always. This is a simulation with a seeded random number generator: evidence, not proof.
spinner.replayNote: “Start again” replays the same spins; “New run” makes new ones.

tenFrame.title: Ten frames
tenFrame.subtitleCount: Tap a box to put a dot in it or take it out. How many dots are there? How many more make ten?
tenFrame.subtitleMakeTen: Fill up the first ten-frame, then see what is left over.
tenFrame.zero: No dots yet. Tap a box to start.

mt.before: {a} dots in the top frame and {b} dots in the bottom frame. How many altogether?
mt.move: Move {k} dots up to fill the top frame. That makes ten, and {rest} stay in the bottom frame.
mt.moveAll: All {b} dots fit in the top frame. Now it has {total} dots.
mt.alreadyTen: The top frame is already a full ten.
mt.legendB: second number ({b}), dots with a hole
mt.diagram: Two ten-frames: {top} dots in the top frame and {bottom} in the bottom frame.

placeValue.title: Base-ten blocks
placeValue.subtitleBuild: Build a number with blocks. Ten small blocks can be traded for one bigger block, and back again.
placeValue.subtitleAdd: Add column by column and see why carrying works: ten blocks of one kind make one block of the next kind.
placeValue.subtitleSubtract: Subtract column by column and see why borrowing works: break one block into ten smaller ones.
placeValue.tooMany: There are {count} {place} in one column. Trade 10 of them for one bigger block to write the number with digits.
placeValue.empty: No blocks yet. Press + to add some.
placeValue.expandedNote: Each digit tells how many blocks are in its column: this is the expanded form of the number.
placeValue.writtenAria: The written column method, step by step

walk.startAdd: Show {a} and {b} with blocks. We add one column at a time, starting with the ones on the right.
walk.startSubtract: Show {a} with blocks. We take away {b} one column at a time, starting with the ones on the right.
walk.swapped: (The larger number goes first, so this is {a} − {b}.)
walk.fits: That fits in one column, so write {digit}.
walk.over: That is more than 9 — too many for one digit.
walk.carry: Write {rest} here, and carry the new block to the next column: that is the little 1 written above it.
walk.notEnough: There are only {have} {place} — not enough to take away {need}.
walk.emptyNext: The next column is empty, so go one column further first.
walk.borrowWrite: In writing, we cross out the digit and write the new number above it.
walk.takeNone: There are no {place} to take away.
walk.doneAdd: Done! The written method does exactly what the blocks did: each carried 1 is a bundle of ten blocks from the column on its right.
walk.doneSubtract: Done! The written method does exactly what the blocks did: each crossed-out digit is a block broken into ten smaller blocks for the column on its right.

subtitle.compare: Each strip is the same whole. Change the fractions and compare how much is shaded.
subtitle.equivalent: Cut every part into the same number of pieces. The pieces change, but the amount stays the same.
subtitle.add: To add or subtract, first cut both wholes into pieces of the same size.
subtitle.line: Every fraction and decimal has its own place on the number line.

fractions.upToTwo: This mode shows values from 0 to 2.
fractions.upToOne: This mode uses fractions from 0 to 1.

compare.why: Cut each whole into {d} equal pieces: then just count the pieces.
compare.equal: They cover exactly the same amount — the fractions are equal.

equiv.explain: Each part is cut into {k} equal pieces. Now {shaded} of {parts} pieces are shaded — still the same amount.
equiv.simplest: This is the simplest form: the pieces cannot be grouped into fewer equal parts.
equiv.family: The same amount, written different ways (tap one):
equiv.onlyFirst: This mode uses only the first fraction.

add.different: The pieces are different sizes (cut into {a} and into {b}), so we can't add or subtract the pieces yet.
add.sameSize: The pieces are already the same size, so we can work with them directly.
add.common: Cut both wholes into {d} equal pieces. Now the pieces are the same size: {d} is a common denominator.
add.combine: Put the pieces together: {a} pieces and {b} pieces make {total} pieces.
add.takeAway: Take {b} pieces away from {a} pieces: {total} pieces are left.
add.swapped: (The larger fraction goes first, so the answer is not negative.)

line.ticks: Cut each whole into equal parts:
line.cantRead: Couldn't read “{s}”. Try a fraction like 3/4, a mixed number like 1 1/2, or a decimal like 0.75.
line.tooBig: {s} is bigger than 2, so it doesn't fit on this line.
line.hint: With {d} equal parts in each whole, which points land exactly on a tick mark?

subtitle.multiples: Mark the multiples of a number and look for patterns. Add a second number to find common multiples.
subtitle.sieve: Cross out the multiples of each prime in turn. The numbers that are never crossed out are the primes.
subtitle.factors: Arrange dots in equal rows. When nothing is left over, you have found a factor pair.
subtitle.gcd: Cut the biggest possible squares from a rectangle, again and again. The side of the last square is the greatest common divisor.

numberGrid.countMultiples: There are {count} multiples of {k} from 1 to {size}.
numberGrid.common: Common multiples of {k} and {k2}: {list}. The smallest one, {lcm}, is the least common multiple.
numberGrid.noCommon: {k} and {k2} have no common multiple up to {size}: the least common multiple is {lcm}.
numberGrid.tapHint: Tap a number to see how it is related.

sieve.start: Here are the numbers from 1 to {size}. Press “Next step” to start sieving.
sieve.one: 1 is not prime: a prime has exactly two factors, and 1 has only one. Cross it out.
sieve.prime: {p} is the next number that is not crossed out, so it is prime. Cross out the other multiples of {p}: {count} new numbers.
sieve.skip: Multiples smaller than {sq} were already crossed out by smaller primes.
sieve.done: Every number still standing is prime: there are {count} primes from 1 to {size}.
sieve.why: We could stop early: every composite number up to {size} has a prime factor no bigger than {root}.
sieve.crossedBy: {m} was crossed out as a multiple of {p}.
sieve.isPrime: {m} is prime: its only factors are 1 and {m}.
sieve.undecided: {m} is not decided yet — keep sieving.

factors.fits: {n} dots make {q} full rows of {r}, with nothing left over: {r} and {q} are factors of {n}.
factors.left: {n} dots make {q} full rows of {r}, with {left} left over: {r} is not a factor of {n}.
factors.pairs: Every rectangle you can make with {n} dots (tap one):
factors.prime: {n} is prime: the only rectangle is a single row.
factors.composite: {n} is composite: it can be arranged in more than one rectangle.
factors.one: 1 has exactly one factor, so it is neither prime nor composite.
factors.square: {n} is a square number: {r} rows of {r} make a square.

gcd.start: A {a} by {b} rectangle. Press “Next step” to cut off the biggest squares that fit.
gcd.cut: {q} squares of side {s} fit, leaving a strip {r} wide.
gcd.exact: {q} squares of side {s} fill what is left exactly.
gcd.done: Squares of side {g} tile the whole rectangle, and no bigger square does: the greatest common divisor of {a} and {b} is {g}.
gcd.equations: Euclid's algorithm, written as division with remainder
gcd.aria: A {a} by {b} rectangle cut into squares

balance.title: Balance the equation
balance.subtitle: Whatever you do to one side, do to the other, and the scale stays level. Get x alone on one side to find its value.
balance.aria: Balance scale: {left} on the left, {right} on the right

reject.noUnits: Not allowed: one side has no 1s to take away. (The same move has to work on both sides.)
reject.noX: Not allowed: one side has no x to take away.
reject.notDivisible: Not allowed: to divide by {k}, every amount on both sides must split into {k} equal groups.
reject.badDivisor: Choose a number from 2 to 9 to divide by.
reject.limit: That would put too many things on the scale.

balance.check: Check it in the first equation:
balance.stuck: The units can't be shared out evenly, so x is not a whole number: x = {frac}.
balance.none: This scale can never balance: both sides have the same number of x's but different numbers of 1s. The equation has no solution.
balance.all: Both sides are the same, so the scale balances whatever x weighs: every number is a solution.
balance.hint: Do the same thing to both sides. Try to get x on its own.
balance.level: The scale is still level: both sides changed by the same amount.

doubleLine.title: Double number line
doubleLine.subtitle: Slide along the two lines: the amounts always stay in the same ratio.
doubleLine.aria: Double number line for the ratio {a} : {b} ({top} and {bottom})
doubleLine.zero: At zero, both amounts are zero.
doubleLine.between: Between the marks the ratio still holds — the amounts can be fractions or decimals.
doubleLine.per: For every 1 on the “{each}” line: {amount} on the “{what}” line.
doubleLine.simplest: Divide both by {g} for the simplest form:

graphx.title: Graph explorer
graphx.subtitle: Dots joined by lines: count degrees, walk along edges, colour vertices, grow spanning trees and count walks with a matrix.
graphx.ignored: {count} malformed vertex or edge entries were skipped.

hint.degrees: Select a vertex to see the edges that meet there.
hint.walk: Click edges one after another to walk along them, or pick a starting vertex first.
hint.colour: Click a vertex to change its colour (Delete removes it).
hint.spanning: Click edges to choose them for a spanning tree.
hint.matrix: Choose a cell of the matrix below.

deg.selected: Vertex {v} has degree {d}: that many edge ends meet there.
deg.handshake: Every edge has two ends, so it adds exactly 2 to the total: the degrees add up to {sum} = 2 × {e}. This is the handshake lemma, Σ deg(v) = 2|E|.
deg.odd: Vertices of odd degree: {count}. This number is always even, because the total is even.

walk.notIncident: That edge does not touch {v}, where your walk is now.
walk.repeated: An edge has been used more than once, so this walk is not a trail.
walk.closed: Closed: it ends where it started
walk.circuit: A closed trail is a circuit.
walk.eulerTrail: Euler trail: every edge exactly once
walk.eulerCircuit: Euler circuit: every edge exactly once, back to the start

euler.circuit: So an Euler circuit exists: whenever a walk enters a vertex, an unused edge is left to leave by. Can you find one?
euler.trail: So an Euler trail exists but no Euler circuit: it must start at one of {a} and {b} and end at the other.
euler.none: So no Euler trail is possible. A trail enters and leaves each vertex in its middle in pairs, so only its two ends can have odd degree, and this graph has {count} such vertices.
euler.disconnected: No Euler trail is possible: the edges fall into separate pieces, and one walk cannot jump between them.
euler.noEdges: This graph has no edges to walk along.

colour.greedyNote: Greedy colouring (largest degree first; each vertex takes the first colour its neighbours have not used) used {k} colours. Greedy is quick, but it does not always find the fewest.
colour.chi: The fewest colours possible for this graph is {k} (its chromatic number), found by a computer search through the colourings.
colour.tooBig: This graph is too big for the quick exhaustive search.
colour.proper: A proper colouring with {k} colours: no edge joins two vertices of the same colour.
colour.clash: Clash: {list}. These edges join two vertices of the same colour.
colour.keepGoing: Give every vertex a colour so that the two ends of each edge differ.
colour.fourColour: This graph is planar: it can be drawn with no edges crossing. The Four Colour Theorem says every planar graph can be coloured with at most four colours. Kenneth Appel and Wolfgang Haken proved it in 1976 with essential help from a computer, which checked well over a thousand cases; in 2005 Georges Gonthier completed a fully computer-checked proof in the Coq proof assistant.
colour.notPlanar: This graph is not planar (it cannot be drawn without edges crossing), so the Four Colour Theorem does not apply to it.

span.count: Edges chosen: {c}. A spanning tree on {v} vertices has exactly {need} edges (|V| − 1).
span.cycle: Your edges contain the cycle {list}; remove one of its edges.
span.pieces: The chosen edges leave {count} separate pieces.
span.treeYes: Connected, no cycles and exactly {need} edges: for a tree, any two of these force the third.
span.disconnectedGraph: This graph is not connected, so it has no spanning tree, only a spanning forest with one tree per piece.
span.tau: Altogether this graph has {tau} different spanning trees (counted exactly by Kirchhoff's matrix-tree theorem).

matrix.edges: A[{a}][{b}] = {count}: the number of edges joining {a} and {b}.
matrix.walks: There are {count} walks of length {k} from {a} to {b}: the entry in row {a}, column {b} of A^{k}.
matrix.pick: Choose a cell: its row is the start vertex, its column the end vertex.
matrix.rowSums: Each row of A adds up to the degree of its vertex.
matrix.diag2: The diagonal of A² repeats the degrees: a walk of length 2 from v back to v goes out along an edge and straight back.
matrix.triangles: trace(A³) = {trace}. Each triangle is counted 6 times (3 starting corners × 2 directions), so this graph has {count} triangles.

truth.title: Truth tables
truth.subtitle: Type a formula of propositional logic and see its value in every possible case.
truth.syntax: Use the symbols ¬ ∧ ∨ → ↔, the words not, and, or, implies, iff, or ASCII ~ & | -> <->. Variables are single lowercase letters. ¬ binds tightest, then ∧, ∨, →, ↔; p → q → r means p → (q → r).

classWhy.contingent: true in {t} of {rows} rows, false in the others.

truth.equivalentWhy: the two formulas agree in all {rows} rows.
truth.rowsNote: {rows} rows: one for every way of making the {vars} variables true or false.

err.empty: Type a formula, for example p → q.
err.tooLong: That formula is too long (at most {max} characters).
err.unknownSymbol: “{symbol}” at position {pos} is not a symbol this table understands.
err.unknownWord: “{word}” at position {pos} is not a variable or an operator. Variables are single lowercase letters, so write p ∧ q rather than pq.
err.unexpected: Unexpected “{symbol}” at position {pos}. Is an operator or a bracket missing?
err.missingOperand: A formula is missing at position {pos}.
err.missingClose: The bracket opened at position {pos} is never closed.
err.tooDeep: That formula is nested too deeply.
err.tooManyVars: This formula has {count} variables; at most {max} fit in a table.

chance.title: Chance lab

sub.coin: Flip a fair coin again and again: the proportion of heads settles towards 1/2. This is the law of large numbers.
sub.dice: Roll one fair die many times and compare the counts with the exact 1/6 for each face.
sub.two-dice: Roll two dice and add them: sums near 7 come up most often, just as counting the 36 outcomes predicts.
sub.galton: Balls bounce left or right at each row of pegs. The bins fill up in a binomial shape, close to a normal curve.
sub.random-walk: Each walker steps left or right at random. The typical distance from the start grows like √n.
sub.birthday: How likely is it that two people in a group share a birthday? Simulate many groups and compare with the exact formula.
sub.monty-hall: Three doors, one car. After the host opens a door with a goat, should you stick or switch?
sub.buffon: Drop needles on a floor ruled with lines one needle-length apart. The chance of crossing a line is 2/π, so needles can estimate π.

axis.rights: number of bounces to the right

legend.switch: switch: share of wins so far
legend.stick: stick: share of wins so far

stat.shared: {c} of {g} groups of {k} shared a birthday
stat.piEstimate: Estimate of π = 2 × needles ÷ crossings (± 95% margin)
stat.piError: Actual error this time: {err}. The margin shrinks only like 1/√N, so one more correct digit needs about 100 times as many needles.

summary.coin: Simulation of {n} flips: {h} heads, proportion {p}. The exact probability is 1/2.
summary.dice: Simulation of {n} rolls: each face came up between {lo} and {hi} of the time. The exact probability is 1/6, about 16.7%.
summary.twoDice: Simulation of {n} rolls of two dice: a sum of 7 came up {p} of the time. The exact probability is 6/36, about 16.7%.
summary.galton: Simulation of {n} balls through {rows} rows: the average bin was {mean}. The exact average is half the number of rows.
summary.walk: Simulation of {w} walks of {n} steps: root-mean-square distance {rms}. The exact value is √n, about {sqrt}.
summary.birthday: Simulated groups of {k} people: {p} had a shared birthday. The exact probability is {e}.
summary.monty: Simulation of {n} games: switching won {sw}, sticking won {stick}. The exact values are 2/3 and 1/3.
summary.buffon: Simulation of {n} needles: π estimated as {est}.

aria.coin: Running proportion of heads over {n} flips, ending at {p}
aria.twoDice: Bar chart of the sums of {n} rolls of two dice, with the exact distribution
aria.galton: Galton board with {rows} rows after {n} balls
aria.walk: Random walk paths over {n} steps, {w} walks in total
aria.birthday: Probability of a shared birthday against group size; for {k} people, simulated {p}, exact {e}
aria.monty: Share of wins over {n} games: stick {stick}, switch {sw}
aria.buffon: {n} needles dropped, {c} of them crossing a line

chance.evidence: This is a simulation of {count} {unit} (run {run}) using a seeded random number generator. It is evidence, not proof: the exact values come from mathematics, and a new run gives slightly different numbers.

note.coin: The proportion settles down, but the difference between the number of heads and n/2 typically grows like √n: the law of large numbers is about proportions, not counts.
note.dice: Small samples are lumpy; the bars even out as the number of rolls grows.
note.twoDice: There are 6 ways to make 7 (1+6, 2+5, 3+4, 4+3, 5+2, 6+1) but only one way to make 12 (6+6).
note.galton: Bin j collects the balls that bounced right j times. C(n, j) of the 2ⁿ equally likely paths lead there, so the exact chance is C(n, j)/2ⁿ. With many rows this binomial shape is close to a normal curve (the central limit theorem).
note.walk: Exactly: the average of (position)² after n steps is n, so the root-mean-square distance is √n. Going twice as far takes four times as many steps.
note.birthday: Exact formula: 1 − (365 × 364 × … × (365 − k + 1)) / 365ᵏ. It assumes 365 equally likely birthdays (no 29 February, no twins). With 23 people the chance first passes 1/2.
note.monty: Your first pick is right with probability 1/3. The host always opens a goat door, so switching wins exactly when your first pick was wrong: probability 2/3. In every game exactly one of the two strategies wins.
note.buffon: The needle length equals the line spacing. The simulation chooses needle directions without using π (it picks random points in a disc), so the estimate does not sneak π in.

play.title: Play it yourself
play.opened: The host opens door {opened}: a goat. Click your door to stick, or door {other} to switch.
play.lost: A goat! The car was behind door {door}.

subtitle.tangent: Shrink h and watch the secant line turn into the tangent: its slope approaches the derivative.
subtitle.riemann: Approximate the area under a curve with thin strips, and watch the error shrink as the strips get thinner.
subtitle.taylor: Polynomials built from the derivatives at 0 hug the function more and more closely, but only inside the interval of convergence.
subtitle.epsdelta: A limit is a promise: for every tolerance ε there is a δ. Choose δ and see whether the graph stays inside the band.

tan.tangentSlope: Slope of the tangent at P
tan.numerical: Numerical estimate (central difference with a tiny step).
tan.hint: As h shrinks, Q slides towards P, the secant turns into the tangent, and its slope settles on the derivative f′(x₀).
tan.corner: Corner at x₀ = {x}: from the left the slopes approach {l}, from the right {r}. No single tangent line fits, so f is not differentiable here.
tan.jump: f jumps at x₀ = {x}. It is not continuous there, so it cannot be differentiable.
tan.vertical: The secant slopes grow without bound as h shrinks: the tangent at x₀ = {x} is vertical, so there is no finite derivative.
tan.undef: f is not defined at x₀ = {x}, or not on both sides of it, so there is no derivative here.
tan.qUndefined: f is not defined at x₀ + h: choose another h.
tan.aria: Graph of f(x) = {f} with the secant line through P at x = {x0} and Q at x = {x1}; its slope is {m}.

riem.hint: Double n and watch the error: left and right sums roughly halve it, midpoint and trapezoid sums cut it to about a quarter.
riem.negative: strips below the axis (hatched) count as negative area
riem.undefined: f is not defined everywhere on [a, b], so these sums do not exist here.
riem.aria: {n} {rule} strips approximating the integral of f(x) = {f} from {a} to {b}; the sum is {sum}.

taylor.convAll: The Taylor series of {f} converges for every real x: at any fixed x, enough terms bring Tₙ(x) as close to f(x) as you like. Far from 0 you simply need more terms.

conv.ln1p: The series converges to ln(1 + x) only for −1 < x ≤ 1. Outside that interval the polynomials peel away from the curve however large n is.
conv.geometric: The series 1 + x + x² + ⋯ converges to 1/(1 − x) only for −1 < x < 1. Outside that interval the polynomials peel away however large n is.
conv.atan: The series converges to arctan x only for −1 ≤ x ≤ 1, even though arctan is smooth everywhere. Outside that interval the polynomials peel away however large n is.

taylor.outside: This x is outside the interval of convergence.
taylor.aria: Graph of f(x) = {f} and its Taylor polynomial of degree {n} about 0.

eps.goal: Your move: find δ > 0 so that every x with 0 < |x − a| < δ satisfies |f(x) − L| < ε.
eps.works: This δ works: on the whole punctured window the graph stays inside the ε-band.
eps.fails: Not yet: near x ≈ {x} the graph leaves the band (|f(x) − L| ≈ {gap}). Try a smaller δ.
eps.evidence: Checked at {count} sample points: evidence, not a proof.
eps.showBest: Show the largest δ that works
eps.best: The largest δ that works is about {d} (numerical search).
eps.noDelta: No δ works for this ε, however small: so the limit is not {L} (or it does not exist).
eps.jump: Try a function with a jump
eps.jumpNote: This function jumps at 0: from the left it approaches −1, from the right +1. Move L anywhere: for ε < 1 no δ works, so the limit at 0 does not exist.
eps.aria: Graph of f(x) = {f} near x = {a}, with the band from {lo} to {hi} and the window from {left} to {right}.

subtitle.arithmetic: Drag z and w. Adding puts arrows end to end; multiplying multiplies lengths and adds angles.
subtitle.roots: The n-th roots of a number c sit evenly spaced on one circle: the corners of a regular polygon.
subtitle.map: See a grid in the z-plane carried to the w-plane. Wherever f′(z) ≠ 0, small right angles stay right angles.
subtitle.winding: How many times does the curve wind around the point p? Count the turns of an arrow, or the signed crossings of a ray.

note.sum: Add the real parts and the imaginary parts separately: z + w is the far corner of the parallelogram built on z and w.
note.product: Multiplying by w stretches by |w| and turns by arg w: lengths multiply and angles add.
note.quotient: Dividing by w shrinks by |w| and turns back by arg w: lengths divide and angles subtract.
note.conjugate: The conjugate reflects z in the real axis: same modulus, opposite argument, and z · z̄ = |z|² is a real number.

complex.wrap: Arguments are given between −180° and 180°, so a whole turn of 360° is added or taken away.
complex.divZero: w = 0: division by zero is undefined.
complex.argZero: 0 has no argument, so only the lengths can be compared.
complex.outside: {name} lies outside the picture; its values are in the table.

roots.heading: Solutions of wⁿ = c for n = {n}:
roots.radius: All roots lie on the circle of radius |c|^(1/n) ≈ {r}.
roots.principal: w₀ is the principal root, at the angle (arg c)/n; the others follow by equal turns.
roots.unity: Because c = 1, these are the roots of unity of order {n}.
roots.sum: The roots add up to 0, so the regular polygon is balanced around the origin.
roots.zero: c = 0: the only solution of wⁿ = 0 is w = 0.

map.legs: small cross at z₀ and its image
map.conformal: Conformal at z₀: the little right angle is turned by {rot} and scaled by {scale}, and it stays a right angle.
map.critical: Here f′(z₀) = 0, so f is not conformal: angles at z₀ are multiplied by {k}, and the right angle opens to {deg}°.
map.pole: z₀ is a pole: f(z₀) is undefined, and images of nearby points run off to infinity.

note.square: Squaring doubles every argument: the right half-plane opens out to the whole plane, and the grid lines become parabolas that still cross at right angles.
note.cube: Cubing triples every argument: the first quadrant opens out to three quarters of the plane. At 0 the angles triple too, so the map is not conformal there.
note.inverse: Inversion turns lines and circles into lines and circles; lines through 0 stay lines, and the unit circle is mapped to itself (reflected).
note.exp: e^(x+iy) = eˣ(cos y + i sin y): vertical lines become circles and horizontal lines become rays. It is conformal everywhere, since f′ = eᶻ is never 0.
note.mobius: A Möbius map: lines and circles go to lines and circles; the imaginary axis becomes the unit circle and the right half-plane becomes the unit disc.
note.joukowski: Circles |z| = r > 1 become ellipses and rays become hyperbolas; the unit circle is flattened onto the segment from −2 to 2. Used to model airflow around wings.

winding.byAngle: By the angle: as the gold point goes once around the curve, the arrow from p turns {k} full turns (counter-clockwise counts as positive).
winding.rayRule: Each crossing of the dashed ray counts +1 where the curve passes upwards (counter-clockwise around p) and −1 where it passes downwards (clockwise).
winding.onCurve: p lies on the curve, where the winding number is not defined. Move it off the curve.
winding.sampled: Both counts are computed on the curve sampled at {count} points.

aria.arithmetic: Complex plane with z = {z}, w = {w} and {op} = {r}.
aria.roots: The {n} roots of c = {c}, on a circle of radius {r}.
aria.wPlane: w-plane: image of the grid under w = {f}; f(z₀) = {w}.

subtitle.slope: Each short segment has the slope dy/dx at its point. Click anywhere to draw the solution through that point.
subtitle.phase: Arrows show where the system moves next. Click to start a trajectory, or choose an example.
subtitle.field: Move the loop through the field: how much does the field circulate around it, flow out of it, and turn along it?

aria.slope: Slope field of dy/dx = {f}, with {count} solution curves.
aria.phase: Phase portrait of x′ = {f}, y′ = {g}, with {count} trajectories.
aria.field: Vector field F = ({f}, {g}) with a circular loop of radius {r} centred at ({cx}, {cy}); index around the loop: {index}.

hint.slope: Click the field to draw a solution, or type a start point below.
hint.phase: Click the plane to start a trajectory, or type a start point below.
hint.field: Drag the gold centre (or click anywhere) to move the loop. With the keyboard, focus the centre and use the arrow keys.

field.rk4: They are numerical approximations (fourth-order Runge–Kutta), not exact formulas.

end.vertical: It stops where its tangent turns vertical: beyond that point it is no longer a function y(x).
end.blowup: It grows so fast that it leaves the picture (it may blow up in finite time).
end.undefined: It stops where f is undefined.
end.closed: The latest trajectory closes up: it is a periodic orbit.
end.cycle: The latest trajectory runs onto a closed loop (to the accuracy of the picture): a periodic orbit or limit cycle.

td.aria: Trace–determinant plane with the classified equilibria marked.
td.caption: Trace T and determinant D: below the T-axis, saddles; above the dashed parabola D = T²/4, spirals; between them, nodes; on the upper D-axis, centres. Left of the D-axis is stable, right is unstable.

kind.degenerate: degenerate: the determinant is 0, so the equilibria are not isolated

field.nonlinear: Nonlinear system. Equilibria found numerically in this window, classified by their linearisation (Jacobian matrix):
field.noEquilibria: No equilibrium found in this window.
field.centerCaveat: A centre of the linearisation is inconclusive for a nonlinear system: the true orbits may close up (as for the pendulum and predator–prey) or spiral slowly.
field.compassAria: Direction of the field at the walking point; turns so far: {turns}.
field.numerical: All values are numerical approximations (sums around the loop and over the disc).

green.ok: circulation = total curl inside, and flux = total divergence inside (up to numerical error).
green.fail: the field must fail to be smooth (or be undefined) somewhere inside the loop, so Green’s theorem does not apply to this loop.

index.undefinedF: The field is undefined somewhere on the loop, so its index is not defined.
index.zero: The field vanishes on the loop, so the index is not defined. Move the loop slightly.
index.near: The field is almost zero somewhere on the loop: a small move of the loop could change the index.
index.nonzero: Index {index} ≠ 0: walking once around the loop, the arrow makes {index} net full turns (negative means clockwise). A non-zero index forces the field to vanish somewhere inside the loop.
index.nonzeroSingular: Index {index} ≠ 0: walking once around the loop, the arrow makes {index} net full turns (negative means clockwise). A field that is continuous on the whole disc would have to vanish inside; this one is not (see above), and the point where it breaks down carries the index instead.
index.none: Index 0: the arrow comes back without a net turn. Nothing is forced: the field may or may not vanish inside the loop.

title.single: How a matrix moves the plane

subtitle.single: Change the entries or pick a transformation. The columns of A are where e₁ and e₂ land; the gold square shows what happens to area.
subtitle.compose: Apply A and then B, or B and then A, and compare the results.

aria.single: The plane transformed by the matrix with rows ({a}, {b}) and ({c}, {d}). The unit square becomes a parallelogram with signed area {det}.
aria.compose: The flag after applying {first} and then {second}, that is, after the matrix {product}.

matrix.morph: From the identity I to A
matrix.morphFlip: Along the way the determinant passes through 0: no continuous motion turns the flag into its mirror image without flattening it at some moment.
matrix.columns: The columns of A are the images of e₁ = (1, 0) and e₂ = (0, 1):

det.area: The unit square (area 1) becomes a parallelogram of area |det A| = {area}.
det.keep: Since det A > 0, orientation is preserved.
det.flip: Since det A < 0, orientation is reversed: the flag is mirrored and the small arc turns clockwise.
det.zero: det A = 0: the whole plane is squashed onto a line or a point, so A has no inverse.

eig.label: Invariant lines (real eigenvectors)
eig.distinct: Vectors on the two dashed lines are only stretched, by the factors λ₁ = {l1} and λ₂ = {l2}; every other direction is turned.
eig.zero: An eigenvalue 0 means that line is crushed to the origin.
eig.negative: A negative eigenvalue flips the vectors on its line to the opposite side.
eig.scalar: Every vector is multiplied by {l}, so every line through 0 is invariant.
eig.defective: Only one invariant line, with eigenvalue {l}: there is no second eigenvector direction.
eig.complex: No real eigenvectors: A turns every direction, so no line through 0 stays put. The eigenvalues are complex.
eig.rotation: In fact A is a rotation by {deg}°.

compose.thenB: First A, then B: the matrix BA
compose.thenA: First B, then A: the matrix AB
compose.equal: Here AB = BA: these two transformations commute.
compose.read: BA means “apply A first, then B”: products of transformations are read from right to left.

subtitle.series: Add the terms one by one. Do the partial sums Sₙ settle down, or keep growing?

seq.band: band from L − ε to L + ε
seq.undefinedAt: The term is undefined at n = {n}.
seq.noLimit: Switch on “Test a limit L” to draw an ε-band around a candidate limit.
seq.found: From n = {N} on, all of the first {M} terms lie within ε = {eps} of L = {L}.
seq.beyond: That index lies beyond the {count} terms plotted: increase the number of terms to see it.
seq.notFound: Terms still leave the band late in the {M} terms checked (the last one at n = {n}), so no index N shows up here: perhaps L is not the limit, or this ε needs more terms.
seq.evidence: Evidence, not proof: a computer can check only finitely many terms. A proof must show |aₙ − L| < ε for every n ≥ N.

aria.sequence: Plot of the terms aₙ = {term} for n from 1 to {count}.
aria.series: Partial sums of the series with terms aₙ = {term}, for n from 1 to {count}.
aria.cobweb: Cobweb diagram for f(x) = {fn}, starting at x₀ = {x0}, with {k} iterations.

aria.fourier: {wave} wave and its Fourier partial sum with {count} terms.

seq.harmonic: This is the harmonic series. Its partial sums grow without bound, but very slowly, like ln n + γ (γ ≈ 0.5772): S₁₀₀₀ ≈ 7.49, and Sₙ first passes 100 only after about 1.5 × 10⁴³ terms. The graph seems to level off; it never does.
seq.termTest: The terms do not seem to approach 0 (|aₙ| is still about {v} at n = {n}). If aₙ does not tend to 0, the series cannot converge: this is the term test.
seq.seriesEvidence: Partial sums on a screen are evidence, never proof: a series can look settled and still diverge, as the harmonic series does.

orbit.fixed: The orbit appears to settle at a fixed point x* ≈ {x}.
orbit.cycle: The orbit appears to settle into a cycle of period {p}: {values}.
orbit.slow: The orbit is still creeping towards a limit (now at x ≈ {x}): convergence here is very slow.
orbit.chaos: No repeating pattern in the first {k} iterates: the orbit may be chaotic.
orbit.escape: The orbit grows without bound: it escapes every bounded region.
orbit.undefined: The orbit reaches a value where f is undefined.

seq.orbitNote: Based on {k} iterations in floating-point arithmetic: numerical evidence, not proof.
seq.peak: highest peak of the partial sum

def.square: f(x) = 1 for 0 < x < π and −1 for −π < x < 0, repeating with period 2π.
def.sawtooth: f(x) = x for −π < x < π, repeating with period 2π.
def.triangle: f(x) = (2/π)·arcsin(sin x): a triangle wave between −1 and 1 with period 2π.

seq.gibbs: Highest peak of the partial sum ≈ {peak}: an overshoot of {over}, which is {pct} % of the jump {jump}.
seq.gibbsNone: With so few terms, the partial sum does not yet overshoot the jump.
seq.gibbsNote: As N grows the overshoot does not shrink to 0: it tends to about 8.95 % of the jump, while the wiggle gets narrower and closer to the jump. This is the Gibbs phenomenon.
seq.uniform: Largest gap between the partial sum and f ≈ {err}. It shrinks as N grows: this series converges uniformly, so there is no overshoot.

euler.title: Vertices, edges and faces
euler.subtitle: Count V, E and F on each solid and work out V − E + F. Then see what holes do.
euler.diagram: {name}, drawn as a see-through wireframe. Solid lines are edges at the front, dashed lines are edges at the back.
euler.dragHint: Drag to turn it. Dashed lines are edges at the back.
euler.countPrompt: Count them yourself — turning the solid helps. Click in a box to highlight what you are counting.
euler.keepCounting: Not all three are right yet. Try turning the solid and counting the back too.
euler.noHoles: No holes: V − E + F = 2. This happens for every solid without holes (Euler's polyhedron formula).
euler.oneHole: This frame has one hole through it, like a doughnut, and V − E + F = 0.
euler.twoHoles: Two holes give V − E + F = −2. Each hole lowers V − E + F by 2.

table.title: Your results
table.note: Counted {done} of {total}. Every solid without holes gives 2; holes change the answer.

surf.intro: Every closed surface with two sides (an inside and an outside) is, up to stretching, a sphere with some number g of handles. That number g is its genus.
surf.handles: Each extra handle lowers χ by 2.
surf.model: One way to cut it into flat faces is the solid “{name}”:
surf.noModel: A frame with three holes would be this surface cut into faces, and it gives V − E + F = −4.
surf.invariant: χ is a topological invariant: it depends only on the surface, not on how you cut it into faces (as long as each face is a disc and faces meet edge to edge).
surf.honest: These examples and moves are evidence, not a proof. Proving that every way of cutting the same surface into faces gives the same χ takes more work — for example, showing that any two ways of cutting it have a common refinement, or using homology.
surf.orientable: The formula χ = 2 − 2g is for closed surfaces with two sides. One-sided surfaces such as the Klein bottle (χ = 0) and the projective plane (χ = 1) need a different formula.

moves.title: Cut it up differently
moves.intro: Make the faces finer. Watch V, E and F change.
moves.edge: Add a vertex in the middle of an edge
moves.diagonal: Cut a face in two with a new edge between two corners
moves.star: Put a vertex inside a face and join it to three corners
moves.note: Each move changes V, E and F, but not V − E + F.
moves.after: {k} moves so far — and V − E + F has not changed.

curved.title: Triangles on curved surfaces
curved.subtitle: Drag the corners. On a flat plane the angles add up to 180°; on a sphere they add up to more, and in the hyperbolic plane to less.

hint.plane: Drag a corner, or focus it and use the arrow keys.
hint.sphere: Drag a corner to move it; drag anywhere else to turn the sphere. The sides are arcs of great circles — the shortest paths on a sphere.
hint.hyperbolic: Poincaré disk model: the sides are arcs of circles that meet the boundary at right angles (dashed: each side extended). The boundary circle is infinitely far away.

curved.planeNote: In the flat plane the three angles always add up to exactly 180°, whatever the shape of the triangle.
curved.sphereNote: On a sphere of radius R, the excess in radians equals the area divided by R². The area is computed separately, by numerical integration, so the match is a check rather than an assumption.
curved.hypNote: In the hyperbolic plane with curvature −1, the defect in radians equals the area. The area is computed separately, by numerical integration.
curved.gaussBonnet: This is a first glimpse of the Gauss–Bonnet theorem: for a triangle whose sides are geodesics (shortest paths), the angle sum minus π equals the total curvature inside it. Here the curvature K is the same everywhere; on other surfaces you add up (integrate) K over the area.
curved.vertex: Corner {name}: drag it, or use the arrow keys to move it
curved.vertexBehind: Corner {name} is on the far side: turn the sphere to see it, or use the arrow keys

diagram.plane: A triangle in the flat plane
diagram.sphere: A triangle on a sphere with great-circle sides. Drag to turn the sphere.
diagram.hyperbolic: A triangle in the Poincaré disk model of the hyperbolic plane

rotate.reset: Centre the view on the triangle

gluing.title: Surfaces from a square
gluing.subtitle: Glue the sides of a square in pairs so that the arrows match. Walk a flatlander across a side and watch where — and how — it comes back.
gluing.keys: Keys: ↑ forward, ↓ back, ← and → turn, Space walks or stops. You can also drag it.
gluing.chiWhy: Gluing turns the 4 corners into V = {v}, the 4 sides into E = 2 and the square into F = 1:

status.normal: Same way round as at the start.
status.mirrored: A mirror image of how it started: its flag has switched sides.

gluing.lastCrossing: Last crossing: out through the {from} side, back in through the {to} side.

about.torus: Opposite sides are glued with arrows pointing the same way. Walk off the right side and you come back on the left, the same way round. However it walks, the flatlander is never mirrored: the torus is orientable.
about.klein: Top and bottom are glued as on the torus, but the left and right sides are glued with opposite arrows. Walk through them and you come back mirrored. A surface on which a walk can mirror you is called non-orientable. The Klein bottle cannot sit in ordinary 3D space without passing through itself.
about.sphere: Here neighbouring sides are glued: fold the square along a diagonal and zip the matching sides shut, like a dumpling. The result is a sphere. Crossing a seam turns the flatlander but never mirrors it.
about.rp2: Both pairs of opposite sides are glued with a twist. This is the real projective plane: non-orientable, with χ = 1. Like the Klein bottle, it cannot sit in 3D space without passing through itself.

gluing.turnNote: Because it is mirrored, a turn to its own left now looks clockwise to us.

tilingNote.torus: Copies of the square tile the plane, and the trail runs on smoothly from copy to copy. This plane is the universal cover of the torus.
tilingNote.klein: For the Klein bottle every other column of copies is flipped upside down (marked ↕), so that neighbouring copies match along the glued sides. The plane is its universal cover too.

gluing.noTiling: There is no flat tiling view for this surface: copies of the square cannot tile the plane consistently, because its universal cover is a sphere, not a plane.

knot.title: Colouring knots with three colours
knot.subtitle: Colour every arc of the diagram. At each crossing, the three arcs that meet must be all the same colour or all different.
knot.arc: Arc {k}: {colour}. Press Enter to change the colour.
knot.howTo: Click an arc to change its colour (or focus it and press Enter, or 1, 2, 3). An arc runs from one under-crossing to the next.

status.trivial: Valid, but it uses only one colour. That always works, so it does not count: a tricolouring must use at least two colours.

knot.searchResult: Of all {total} ways to colour the arcs of this diagram, {valid} obey the rule at every crossing, and {trivial} of those use a single colour.
knot.searchYes: One that uses all three colours is shown.
knot.searchNo: None uses more than one colour, so this diagram — and therefore every diagram of this knot or link — cannot be tricoloured.
knot.linking: Linking number (its sign depends on the directions chosen)
knot.rule: Why this rule? Any two diagrams of the same knot are related by three kinds of local moves, the Reidemeister moves: adding or removing a twist, sliding one strand over another, and sliding a strand past a crossing. Each move turns a valid colouring with two or more colours into another one.
knot.invariant: So tricolourability is a knot invariant: if one diagram of a knot can be tricoloured, every diagram of it can. A plain circle has just one arc, so the unknot cannot be tricoloured.

about.unknot: This diagram has a crossing, but untwisting it (a Reidemeister move) removes it: the unknot has crossing number 0. With only one arc, every colouring uses one colour.
about.trefoil: The trefoil can be tricoloured and the unknot cannot. Because tricolourability is an invariant, no amount of wiggling turns the trefoil into the unknot: the trefoil really is knotted.
about.figureEight: The figure-eight knot cannot be tricoloured — just like the unknot. Yet it is knotted, as other invariants (such as the Jones polynomial) prove. When an invariant gives the same answer for two knots it proves nothing: invariants can fail to tell knots apart.
about.hopf: Two linked rings. The Hopf link cannot be tricoloured, while two separate rings can (give each ring its own colour), so the rings cannot be pulled apart. Its linking number, ±1 instead of 0, proves the same thing.
about.cinquefoil: The cinquefoil, or 5₁ knot, cannot be tricoloured, so this test cannot tell it apart from the unknot. It is knotted all the same, as other invariants show.

winding.title: Winding around a hole
winding.subtitle: Follow a closed loop and count how many times it goes around each hole: counter-clockwise turns minus clockwise turns.
winding.diagram: The plane with holes and a closed loop. A point travels along the loop; dashed arrows join each hole to the point.
winding.puncture: Hole {k}: drag it, or move it with the arrow keys
winding.hint: Drag a hole to move it. Press Play to send the point around the loop, or use the slider. The small square marks the start.
winding.drawHint: Draw a loop with your finger or mouse; it closes itself when you let go. (With a keyboard, choose one of the ready-made loops.)
winding.through: The loop passes through {p}, so the winding number is not defined. Move the hole or the loop.
winding.swept: Turns swept so far by each dashed arrow:
winding.howComputed: The winding number is found by adding up the small changes in direction of the arrow from the hole to the moving point, and dividing the total by 360°. Counter-clockwise counts as positive.
winding.homotopy: Two loops in the plane with one hole can be deformed into each other, without ever crossing the hole, exactly when they have the same winding number. In the language of topology: the fundamental group of the punctured plane — like that of a circle — is the integers, π₁ = ℤ.
winding.twoHoles: With two holes, the winding numbers around each hole are still invariants, but they no longer tell the whole story. The fundamental group is now the free group on two generators: a loop that goes around p₁, then p₂, then p₁ backwards, then p₂ backwards winds 0 times around each hole, yet it cannot be shrunk to a point.
winding.complex: A link to complex analysis: think of the plane as the complex numbers and of a hole as a point a. Then (1/2πi)∮ dz/(z − a) equals the winding number around a. The values above are computed numerically along the loop.

curvature.title: The curvature of a curve
curvature.subtitle: A point travels along the curve. The osculating circle is the circle that fits the curve best at that point; its radius is 1/κ.
curvature.diagram: The {name}, with the moving point, its unit tangent T, its unit normal N and the osculating circle
curvature.handle: Control point {k}: drag it, or move it with the arrow keys

param.b: Height b of the ellipse (its width is 4)

curvature.bezierHint: Drag the square control points to reshape the curve.
curvature.signNote: κ is positive where the curve bends to the left as you travel along it, and negative where it bends to the right. N is the tangent T turned 90° to the left; the centre of the osculating circle lies 1/|κ| away, on the side the curve bends towards.
curvature.openTotal: This curve is not closed, so ∫ κ ds is just the total turn of the tangent from start to end — about {deg}° — and need not be a whole number of turns.
curvature.closedTotal: Turning number {k}: going once around, the tangent turns through {k} × 360° in total.
curvature.cusp: This curve has a cusp, where it stops and turns back, so it is not smooth there. Over the smooth part ∫ κ ds = 3π. At the cusp the tangent flips by half a turn, which counts as −π, and the total is again 2π — as the Umlaufsatz for curves with corners predicts.
curvature.umlaufsatz: Hopf's Umlaufsatz: for a smooth closed curve, ∫ κ ds = 2π × (turning number). A simple closed curve — one that never crosses itself — traversed counter-clockwise always has turning number 1. The limaçon with an inner loop has 2; the figure eight has 0.
curvature.bezierCusp: With these control points the curve has a cusp (a point where it momentarily stops), and κ blows up there.
curvature.numeric: Arc length and ∫ κ ds are computed numerically from exact derivatives at thousands of points, so the last digit may wobble.
curvature.graph: Signed curvature κ against arc length s
curvature.graphLabel: Graph of the signed curvature of the {name} against arc length
curvature.graphNote: The signed area under this graph is ∫ κ ds (teal above the axis counts as positive, terracotta below as negative). Very large values near a cusp are cut off.
